slides.title: The Attribution Framework shows the white space.
slides.headline: The Attribution Framework shows the white space.
slides.support: It compares your whole company with your competitors, across your market.
body: Where does everyone compete on the same thing?
Where is the white space between you and your best competitor?
Where will you be in 3 years?
notes: Strategy is a unique and valuable position. You get there by moving into white space that matters to your Core Customer.
This is about the company, not a product.
It is a key strategic picture. Give it time, and let the team sleep on it.
Allow about 60 minutes.

artwork.alt: A simple chart with two lines. A solid green line is you, in 3 years. A dashed line is your best competitor. The space between the two lines is white on a gray ground, and is marked white space.

slides.title: Attributes: how everyone on your Market Map compares companies.
slides.headline: Attributes: how everyone on your Market Map compares companies.
notes: An attribute is something the market compares companies on.
Anyone with power on your Market Map weighs attributes: buyers, channels, influencers and acquirers.
Include attributes nobody competes on yet. No customer can ask for those.
Keep it at company level. Do not list product features.
Aim for 12 to 15 attributes.

Security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network follow. Scores run from 1 to 5. Every line is dimmed and the attribute names are bright. Callout: Why: the market sets the attributes, not our product. Ask: what describes the whole market?

slides.title: Example: the company scores itself, 1 to 5.
slides.headline: Example: the company scores itself, 1 to 5.
notes: Score how well the company serves each attribute today, from 1 to 5.
Order the attributes from best to worst. The line then falls from left to right.
Score today honestly. A company with no 5s has room to grow.

slides.headline: Example: the top competitors, on the same attributes.
notes: Score two or three competitors on the same attributes, in the same order.
If the team cannot score a competitor with confidence, stop. Assign the research as homework.
Look for where every line bunches together. That is where everyone competes on the same thing.

They start with speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity and support from a person. Callout: Why: the lines show where everyone competes. Ask: how would each competitor score?

slides.title: White space is the gap between you and your best competitor.
slides.headline: White space is the gap between you and your best competitor.
notes: White space is the gap between the company and its best competitor on an attribute. It can be above the competitor line or below it.
The dashed line is the highest of the competitor scores on each attribute. Where the two lines touch, the company competes head on.
Today’s gaps were not chosen. In the example the company leads a little on the left and trails on the right without having decided to.
The 3HAG line is where the team chooses its white space. That is the next slide.
Ask the team where the white space is before you point at it.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the example subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom, from speed of setup to partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. A solid line shows Us today. A dashed line shows the best competitor score on each attribute. The space between the two lines is white on a gray ground. On the left the company is a little above its best competitor. On the right it is well below. Where the two lines touch there is no white.

slides.title: Your 3HAG line opens your white space.
slides.headline: Your 3HAG line opens your white space.
notes: The 3HAG line is where the company will be in 3 years on each attribute. Decide where to invest, what to maintain and what to give up.
White space takes investment, and the company does not have unlimited funds. What it gives up pays for what it invests in. It does not overextend.
A good 3HAG line gives something up. If every score goes up, go again. Do not force it on the first round.
Competitors can copy what you add. They cannot copy what you drop without breaking their own business.
In the example, reporting and customization drop, so that setup, price and support can lead.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the example subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. A green 3HAG line and a dashed Best competitor line cross the chart. The space between them is white on a gray ground. On the left the 3HAG line is above the competitor line, at 5 on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person. That white is marked Invest. On the right the 3HAG line drops below it, to 2 on reporting and 1 on customization. That white is marked Give up. Where the two lines touch, on ease of use and reliability, there is no white. A faint line shows Us today.

slides.support: It is where you will be in 3 years. You invest to lead in some places and pay for it by giving up others.

slides.title: What are the attributes of your market?
slides.headline: What are the attributes of your market?
slides.support: Start from everyone on your Market Map.
body: On your own, write 5 to 7 things your market compares companies on.
Share them. Group the ones that mean the same thing, and name each group.
Finish with 12 to 15 attributes as a team.
notes: Each leader works in private. Show your answers, then agree.
In a small team, each person writes 7 to 10. The team then still ends with 12 to 15 after grouping.
Keep the attributes about the whole market, not one customer.
Think beyond the buyer. Channels, influencers and acquirers weigh attributes too.
Allow about 20 minutes.

slides.title: Score your company and your competitors.
slides.headline: Score your company and your competitors.
slides.support: One person copies the Attribution Map sheet and enters your attributes.
body: Score your company and two or three competitors, 1 to 5.
Everyone scores alone first. The CEO shares last.
Enter the agreed scores. The graph sorts itself.
Then ask: where is the white space?
notes: Scan the code, then choose File and Make a copy in Google Sheets. One person shares the copy on screen.
Each leader writes scores in private. Then compare them, and the CEO shares last.
The spread between scores is where the discussion is.
Enter scores in any order. The sheet orders the attributes from best to worst. Keep 3 competitors on the sheet, so the 3HAG line keeps its own style.
The first pass is directional. Do not argue decimals.
Then ask: where is the white space?

The sheet draws two charts. The first is the Attribution Map. Under it, the White Space chart shows the gap between the 3HAG line and the best competitor. It fills in once the team enters its 3HAG line.
Allow about 25 minutes.

notes: This is what the sheet looks like once the scores are in. The numbers are the example company’s, the same as on the example graph.
Leave the 3HAG Line column empty for now. The team fills it in when it draws the 3HAG line.
Enter the attributes in any order. The sheet sorts them from best to worst for the chart.
Under the first chart the sheet draws a second one, White Space. It needs the 3HAG Line column, so it is empty until the team draws its line.

slides.title: Which white space matters to your Core Customer?
slides.headline: Which white space matters to your Core Customer?
slides.support: Put your Core Customer on the screen. Does each patch of white space serve one of their three ranked needs?
notes: Put the team’s own Core Customer on the screen. The example here is a reminder of its parts.
Read their three ranked needs aloud. For each patch of white space, ask: does it serve one of those needs? Keep the white space that does. Set the rest aside.
The white space only counts if it matters to the Core Customer.
Use the team’s own Core Customer, from wherever the team keeps it. In Metronome it belongs on a wall in the War Room, which starts empty until the team adds walls.
Hold each patch of white space against the needs. The ones that serve a need are where the 3HAG line can lead.
Change only what is no longer true about the Core Customer.
Homework: update the Core Customer in the War Room in Metronome.

artwork.alt: An example Core Customer for the subscription company. Core Customer: owner of a small business. Description: the owner of a business with 10 to 50 staff. They decide alone, pay by card, and want it working this month without an IT person. Prioritized needs. 1, up and running in days. 2, a cost they can predict. 3, a person to call when stuck. Prioritized benefits. 1, live in 5 days or fewer. 2, one flat monthly price. 3, a named contact for 90 days. Persona: Dana, owner of a 20-person business. Revenue 55%, profit 60%.

slides.title: Draw your 3HAG line.
slides.headline: Draw your 3HAG line.
slides.support: Decide where to invest, what to maintain and what to give up.
body: Enter a 3HAG score for each attribute.
Ask: what will we be worse at in 3 years?
notes: In the example, Dana needs fast setup, a predictable cost and a person to call. The 3HAG line leads on all three.
What the team gives up pays for what it invests in. Then look at the White Space chart on the sheet: is there enough white between the 3HAG line and the best competitor?
Let the team sleep on it. The line can change before the annual.
Homework: add the Attribution Framework to the War Room in Metronome.

slides.title: What does the white space change?
slides.headline: What does the white space change?
body: What should become a priority this quarter?
What will you stop doing because the 3HAG line drops it?
notes: Write the answers on the board. They become candidates when the team builds the QHAG.
Next, test the 3HAG and the 1HAG with these answers, then build the QHAG.
A team that runs out of time finishes the Attribution Framework in an extra session before the annual.
